Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Thinking Like a Child to Unlock Creative Solutions.
Picture the way children see the world. There’s this sense of wonder, and they aren’t afraid to ask questions that adults might brush off as silly or naive. But here’s the thing—this childlike curiosity can be a real superpower, especially when you’re stuck and the usual ways just aren’t working.
As adults, we carry around a lot of experience. Sometimes, that’s awesome—it means we know stuff and can make smart decisions. But it can also trip us up. The more we think we “know,” the less likely we are to question the basics or entertain off-the-wall ideas that could actually work.
So, what does it really mean to think like a child? Well, it’s about coming at problems with curiosity instead of judgment. It’s about daring to ask those simple, direct questions—even if you worry they’ll sound foolish. And it’s about being open to try things out, mess up, and learn as you go.
This way of thinking can lead to breakthroughs that more experienced folks might just overlook. Imagine a kid asking, “Why does this vending machine only take coins?” Suddenly, you’re thinking about new payment options. Or maybe a child wonders why school starts so early, and that sparks a bigger conversation about how sleep affects learning.
In creative fields, this mindset is gold. Artists, inventors, and entrepreneurs are often celebrated for seeing the world with fresh eyes. But honestly, this approach can make a difference in everyday life, too. When you stop worrying about always looking like the expert, you open yourself up to exploring new possibilities and challenging the usual way of doing things.
Now, if you’re wondering how to actually develop this mindset, here’s a simple trick: practice asking “why” over and over. Every answer you get, hit it with another “why.” It’s called the “five whys” technique, and it’s a powerful way to dig past the obvious and find what’s really going on.
Another great move? Get input from people who see things differently. Kids, newcomers, people who aren’t insiders—they often spot things the rest of us miss. So, invite their questions and take them seriously. You might be surprised at the hidden opportunities you’ll uncover.
Of course, I’m not saying you should ignore everything you know or toss out your expertise. It’s about finding a balance—combining your knowledge with genuine curiosity. Stay open to new ideas, even if they sound a little out there.
In real life, this might look like setting aside time for judgment-free brainstorming, or encouraging everyone on your team—no matter how new or experienced—to ask questions. And sometimes, it means giving an unlikely idea a shot, just to see what happens.
Over time, this way of thinking can turn into a culture of innovation and steady improvement. When you mix the curiosity of a child with the wisdom of an adult, you open the door to solving problems in ways most people would never even think of.
